existingLink.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
existingLink.anchor: Where federal law let highway money go to transit (1992 to 2006), states spent about 3% of the whole federal-aid highway program on transit, 13% of the flexible part; California put nearly 40% of its flexible money there, and 19 states less than 2%. The same 3% of a state's own highway spending (Census Bureau, 2022: $128.0 billion) is 5.9% of what transit agencies spend to run service (FTA National Transit Database, 2024: $65.6 billion), so service rises about 6% at the average cost per mile. The spread takes 2% to 40% of the flexible part. The lag is a budget cycle and the buses it buys, the most common use GAO found.
existingLink.source: GAO-07-772, Highway and Transit Investments: Flexible Funding Supports State and Local Transportation Priorities (2007); Census Bureau, 2022 Census of Governments: Finance, Table 1 (state highways); FTA National Transit Database 2024 (data.transportation.gov ekg5-frzt, total operating expenses)

existingLink.per: law in force says yes (1) rather than no (0)
existingLink.anchor: Transit ridership's elasticity with respect to fares is -0.2 to -0.5 in the first year. A fare falling to zero is read on the semi-log curve the paper recommends for fares near zero, where ridership rises by e to the elasticity: 22% to 65%, 42% at the middle of the range. Long-run elasticities of -0.6 to -0.9 would give more, so this is the first year's effect, held.
existingLink.source: Litman 2025, Transit Price Elasticities and Cross-Elasticities, Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Table 15 and page 9

why: Removing a fare changes the price a covered rider pays.
A rider may choose a trip if its route, timing, destination and alternatives meet their recorded needs.

bedrock.kind: price incentive, missing personal trip decision

existingLink.per: percent a law or other cause moved the place's transit service (vehicle revenue miles per resident)
existingLink.anchor: Each 1% more transit service raises ridership about 0.5%: the elasticity with respect to service frequency averages 0.5, typical urban systems with 30-minute or better headways run about 0.30, and expanding routes into new areas typically gives 0.6 to 1.0. New service takes 1 to 3 years to reach its full ridership, so this acts from the first year. Only the part of service that laws and other causes moved is read, so service's own drift, which ridership's drift already stands for, is not counted twice.
existingLink.source: Litman, Transit Price Elasticities and Cross-Elasticities, Victoria Transport Policy Institute, June 17, 2025, page 12 (Service Elasticities), https://www.vtpi.org/tranelas.pdf
